hypotheses.title: LSASS Handle with Credential-Access Memory Mask
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor with elevated access on Windows is suspected of reading lsass.exe process memory to extract authentication material. Hunt for non-system processes opening handles to lsass.exe with credential-access or all-access masks, particularly when CallTrace includes UNKNOWN or unexpected DLLs indicating direct syscall or manual API use.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 10
pivots.detail: TargetImage = lsass.exe AND GrantedAccess IN (0x1010, 0x1038, 0x1400, 0x1410, 0x1438, 0x143a, 0x1fffff, 0x1f0fff) AND SourceImage NOT IN (WerFault.exe, WerFaultSecure.exe, Sysmon64.exe, MsMpEng.exe, csrss.exe)

pivots.label: CallTrace anomaly
pivots.detail: CallTrace containing UNKNOWN = direct syscall (NanoDump, custom loaders). CallTrace ending in dbgcore.dll or dbghelp.dll = debugging API path used by ProcDump and older Mimikatz. Modern Mimikatz routes through ntdll.dll alone.

pivots.label: Timing & frequency
pivots.detail: LSASS access >30 min after the last user logon, from a process with no prior LSASS access history, or clustered with 5+ unique source processes within 10 minutes — all significantly raise confidence.

hypotheses.fpr: AV/EDR products, WerFault.exe, Sysmon itself, and tools such as Process Explorer all legitimately access LSASS. Exclude by signed binary + known install path. Alert only when SourceImage is not in an org-maintained allowlist.

hypotheses.title: comsvcs.dll MiniDump Abuse via rundll32
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of abusing the comsvcs.dll MiniDumpW export (ordinal #24) via rundll32.exe to dump LSASS memory without deploying external tools. Hunt for rundll32.exe command lines combining comsvcs with MiniDump or ordinal references (#24, #65560) alongside a PID or the string 'lsass'.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1
pivots.detail: Image = rundll32.exe AND CommandLine contains (comsvcs.dll OR comsvcs) AND CommandLine contains (MiniDump OR #24 OR #65560 OR full)

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 10
pivots.detail: TargetImage = lsass.exe AND CallTrace contains comsvcs.dll AND GrantedAccess = 0x1fffff. Correlate with an EID 1 for rundll32 within 2 seconds of the access event.

pivots.label: PowerShell variant
pivots.detail: comsvcs.dll can be invoked from PowerShell via Start-Process or a direct COM call. Also hunt: EID 4104 ScriptBlockText contains 'MiniDump' AND 'comsvcs'.

hypotheses.fpr: No legitimate administrative use case invokes comsvcs.dll MiniDump against lsass.exe. This detection has near-zero FPR. Confirm by checking for output .dmp file creation within seconds of the rundll32 event.

hypotheses.title: SysInternals ProcDump Targeting LSASS
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of using the legitimate SysInternals ProcDump utility to write a full LSASS memory dump to disk for offline credential extraction. Hunt for procdump.exe or procdump64.exe process creation with command-line arguments naming lsass by name or PID, especially when executed from non-standard paths or by unusual parent processes.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1
pivots.detail: Image endswith (procdump.exe OR procdump64.exe) AND (CommandLine contains '-ma lsass' OR CommandLine contains '-mm lsass' OR CommandLine contains lsass.exe)

pivots.label: Parent process
pivots.detail: ProcDump launched from cmd.exe, powershell.exe, wmiexec, or psexec parent is highly suspicious. ProcDump executing from a UNC path (\\server\share\) indicates remote tool staging.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 11
pivots.detail: File created by procdump.exe with .dmp extension in a temp or user-writable directory within seconds of process creation confirms a dump was successfully written.

hypotheses.fpr: ProcDump is a legitimate SysInternals tool used by developers and Microsoft support. Allowlist execution from C:\Program Files when the target is not lsass and the parent is a recognized IDE or support session. Alert on: lsass target, unusual parent, staging path, off-hours.

hypotheses.title: LSASS Dump File Creation in Staging Path
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of having successfully dumped LSASS memory to a file in a staging path for subsequent exfiltration. Hunt for .dmp or custom-extension files created in world-writable or temp directories by any process with prior LSASS handle activity, or by Task Manager (low-tech operator dump technique).

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 11
pivots.detail: TargetFilename endswith .dmp AND (TargetFilename contains lsass OR Image endswith taskmgr.exe OR Image endswith procdump.exe OR Image endswith rundll32.exe) AND TargetFilename matches (%TEMP%\* OR C:\Windows\Temp\* OR C:\ProgramData\* OR %APPDATA%\*)

pivots.label: File size heuristic
pivots.detail: LSASS memory dumps are typically 30–150 MB. A large .dmp file in %TEMP%, AppData\Local, or C:\Windows\Temp created outside a crash scenario is a strong indicator — correlate file size with creation process.

pivots.label: Task Manager variant
pivots.detail: Image = taskmgr.exe AND TargetFilename contains lsass AND TargetFilename endswith .dmp — this covers the low-tech manual dump technique documented in PYSA/Mespinoza campaigns.

refs.label: DFIR Report — PYSA Task Manager dumps

hypotheses.fpr: WerFault.exe and WerFaultSecure.exe legitimately create LSASS-related crash dumps — exclude those processes. Developer crash dump sessions may produce .dmp files in custom paths; correlate with active debugging sessions and approved tooling.

hypotheses.title: Encoded PowerShell with Execution-Policy Bypass Flags
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of using encoded PowerShell commands combined with execution-policy bypass flags to conceal payload content from casual inspection and evade script-block logging on unpatched hosts. Hunt for powershell.exe spawned with -enc or -EncodedCommand alongside -NoP, -NonI, -W Hidden, or -Exec Bypass.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1
pivots.detail: Image endswith powershell.exe AND CommandLine contains (-enc OR -EncodedCommand) AND CommandLine contains (-nop OR -NonInteractive OR hidden OR bypass)

pivots.label: Decode and inspect
pivots.detail: Decode the -enc argument (Base64). If the plaintext contains IEX, DownloadString, Invoke-*, reflection patterns, or AmsiUtils — escalate. SIEM enrichment or CyberChef recipes can automate decode at alert time.

pivots.label: String length heuristic
pivots.detail: Legitimate admin encoded commands are typically <500 characters. Payloads >1,500 characters post-Base64 often represent multi-layer compressed or obfuscated payloads and should be decoded and reviewed.

hypotheses.fpr: SCCM, Intune, and GPO delivery scripts often use encoding for safe transport. Allowlist by: signed binary, scheduled task context, execution from C:\Windows\System32 or C:\Program Files, known admin workstation. Baseline encoded PS frequency per host — spikes indicate anomalous activity.

hypotheses.title: In-Memory Download Cradle (Fileless Execution)
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of using a PowerShell download cradle — Net.WebClient.DownloadString or Invoke-WebRequest piped into IEX — to fetch and execute a remote payload entirely in memory, leaving no file on disk. Hunt for ScriptBlock log events containing both a web-client download method and an invocation expression within the same or consecutive events.

pivots.label: PS EID 4104 — primary
pivots.detail: ScriptBlockText contains (DownloadString OR DownloadData OR WebClient) AND ScriptBlockText contains (IEX OR Invoke-Expression OR &([scriptblock]::Create))

pivots.label: Network correlation
pivots.detail: Correlate EID 4104 match with Sysmon EID 3 (Network) from powershell.exe to the same destination within ±5 seconds. Non-browser PS network connections to external IPs or newly-registered domains warrant automatic escalation.

pivots.label: User-Agent baseline
pivots.detail: Default PowerShell UA: 'Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT; ...) WindowsPowerShell/5.1.X'. Any deviation — custom UA, no UA, or curl-like strings — from a PS-initiated connection is a strong indicator.

pivots.label: Obfuscated variant
pivots.detail: Attackers split 'DownloadString' across variables or use character arrays. Hunt for Net.WebClient in ScriptBlock text as a stable anchor and flag any block where the content is followed within 5 seconds by a second high-entropy ScriptBlock event.

refs.label: DFIR Report — Cobalt Strike staging chains
Elastic: execution via PowerShell download cradle

hypotheses.fpr: Legitimate admin scripts use Invoke-WebRequest to pull resources from known CDNs, GitHub, or internal update servers. Allowlist by destination domain: Microsoft, GitHub, corporate update infrastructure. Alert on unknown or new destination domains regardless of protocol.

hypotheses.title: AMSI Bypass via PowerShell Reflection
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of patching the AMSI scan interface in memory using .NET reflection to disable antimalware scanning before executing a concealed payload. Hunt for ScriptBlock log events containing AmsiUtils, amsiInitFailed, or reflection-based SetValue calls targeting System.Management.Automation assemblies.

pivots.label: PS EID 4104 — direct
pivots.detail: ScriptBlockText contains (AmsiUtils OR amsiInitFailed) OR (ScriptBlockText contains System.Management.Automation AND ScriptBlockText contains SetValue AND ScriptBlockText contains amsi)

pivots.label: PS EID 4104 — Obfuscated
pivots.detail: ScriptBlockText contains [Ref].Assembly.GetType AND System.Management.Automation AND SetValue. Also: character-array construction of 'AmsiUtils' using [cHAr] concatenation, or -replace and -join patterns that reconstruct the class name at runtime.

pivots.label: Behavioral follow-up
pivots.detail: An AMSI bypass is almost always followed within seconds by a second ScriptBlock executing the concealed payload. A gap <5 seconds between a ScriptBlock containing AmsiUtils and a second high-entropy or offensive-cmdlet ScriptBlock = confirmed evasion chain.

hypotheses.fpr: Authorized security testing frameworks and some EDR products may interact with AMSI internals. In production environments outside approved red team windows, legitimate AMSI bypass activity is essentially zero — alert on any occurrence and investigate promptly.

hypotheses.title: Offensive Framework Cmdlets via ScriptBlock Logging
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of executing PowerShell-based offensive framework modules — from PowerSploit, PowerView, Empire, or Mimikatz — captured in ScriptBlock logs. Hunt for EID 4104 events containing known offensive cmdlet names across credential dumping, lateral movement, AD enumeration, and defense evasion categories.

pivots.label: Credential dumping
pivots.detail: ScriptBlockText contains (Invoke-Mimikatz OR Invoke-NinjaCopy OR Get-GPPPassword OR Invoke-Kerberoast OR Invoke-DCSync OR Get-Credential OR Out-Minidump)

pivots.label: Lateral movement
pivots.detail: ScriptBlockText contains (Invoke-PsExec OR Invoke-WMICommand OR Invoke-SMBExec OR Invoke-TheHash OR New-PSDrive.*IPC OR Enter-PSSession)

pivots.label: Discovery & enumeration
pivots.detail: ScriptBlockText contains (Invoke-BloodHound OR Get-DomainAdmin OR Find-DomainShares OR Invoke-UserHunter OR Get-NetComputer OR Get-NetUser) — AD enumeration cmdlets characteristic of BloodHound/PowerView reconnaissance.

pivots.label: Defense evasion
pivots.detail: ScriptBlockText contains (Set-MpPreference -Disable* OR Remove-MpPreference OR Invoke-BypassUAC OR Invoke-TokenManipulation OR Add-Persistence)

refs.label: CISA AA25-141A — Akira PS credential dumping

hypotheses.fpr: PowerShell ScriptBlock logging (EID 4104) must be enabled via GPO — without it these events do not exist. The listed cmdlets are exclusively offensive with no legitimate administrative use. FPR is near-zero; any match warrants immediate investigation.

hypotheses.title: Remote Thread Injection into High-Privilege Host Process
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of injecting a malicious payload into a trusted host process (svchost.exe, explorer.exe, lsass.exe) via CreateRemoteThread or NtCreateThreadEx to execute shellcode in a high-integrity context. Hunt for Sysmon EID 8 events where the source process is not a known debugging tool and the target is a system process, especially when the StartAddress falls outside any mapped image region.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 8
pivots.detail: SourceImage NOT IN (devenv.exe, dbgview.exe, vsjitdebugger.exe, msvsmon.exe) AND TargetImage IN (svchost.exe, explorer.exe, lsass.exe, winlogon.exe, spoolsv.exe) AND StartFunction is null or StartModule is null (unbacked thread start address)

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — parent anomaly
pivots.detail: Unusual parent-child pairs preceding injection: cmd.exe or powershell.exe spawning a process that then triggers EID 8. Correlate source PID in EID 8 with a prior EID 1 showing the loader process was created from a suspicious parent.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 10 — pre-injection handle
pivots.detail: TargetImage IN (svchost.exe, explorer.exe) AND GrantedAccess IN (0x1fffff, 0x1f0fff, 0x40, 0x43a) — PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS or PROCESS_VM_WRITE + PROCESS_VM_OPERATION rights obtained by a non-system source process within 5 seconds of an EID 8 on the same target PID.

hypotheses.fpr: Legitimate debuggers (devenv.exe, vsjitdebugger.exe, windbg.exe) use remote thread creation routinely. EDR agents themselves may inject threads into monitored processes. Exclude signed binaries from known vendors at well-known install paths; alert only on unbacked or unsigned source processes.

hypotheses.title: Process Hollowing via Suspended-Process + WriteProcessMemory
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of hollowing out a legitimate process by spawning it in a suspended state, unmapping its memory, and writing a malicious image prior to resumption — a technique used to masquerade malicious execution as a trusted binary. Hunt for Sysmon EID 8 where the started thread address resolves outside the target process's main image, combined with a preceding EID 1 showing the target was spawned with CREATE_SUSPENDED semantics (often reflected in unusual parent context or process start time delta).

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 8 — StartModule null
pivots.detail: SourceImage != TargetImage AND StartModule is null AND TargetImage IN (svchost.exe, notepad.exe, msiexec.exe, regsvr32.exe, dllhost.exe) — unbacked start address indicates the original PE was replaced.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4688 — CommandLine audit
pivots.detail: NewProcessName endswith svchost.exe AND ParentProcessName NOT IN (services.exe, MsMpEng.exe) — svchost.exe created by anything other than services.exe is a near-certain indicator of process hollowing or phantom process launch.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 + EID 8 correlation
pivots.detail: EID 1: Image = svchost.exe (or msiexec.exe) spawned by a user-mode process (e.g., explorer.exe, cmd.exe). Within 2 seconds, EID 8 originates from the same parent writing a remote thread into the newly created child. Sequence is characteristic of RunPE / process hollowing loaders.

hypotheses.fpr: Windows Installer (msiexec.exe) and COM surrogate (dllhost.exe) are legitimately launched by various orchestrators; key discriminator is the parent process. Svchost.exe parent must always be services.exe — any deviation has near-zero legitimate justification. Tune on environment-specific orchestration tooling.

hypotheses.title: DLL Injection via LoadLibrary Path Planted by Adversary
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of using WriteProcessMemory + CreateRemoteThread with a LoadLibrary call to force a target process to load an adversary-controlled DLL from a world-writable or user-controlled path. Hunt for Sysmon EID 7 (image load) events where a DLL loaded into a high-privilege process originates from a non-standard path and is unsigned or signed by an untrusted certificate.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 7 — image load
pivots.detail: Image IN (svchost.exe, explorer.exe, lsass.exe) AND ImageLoaded NOT startswith (C:\Windows\System32, C:\Windows\SysWOW64, C:\Program Files) AND Signed = false OR SignatureStatus != Valid

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 8 — LoadLibrary address
pivots.detail: StartFunction = LoadLibraryA OR StartFunction = LoadLibraryW AND TargetImage IN (explorer.exe, notepad.exe, svchost.exe) — StartFunction resolves to LoadLibrary when the injector uses the classic technique.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — staging
pivots.detail: Unsigned DLL dropped to %TEMP%, %APPDATA%, C:\ProgramData, or C:\Users\Public within 60 seconds before EID 7 showing the same filename loaded into a host process. Correlate by filename and directory.

hypotheses.fpr: Third-party software frequently loads DLLs from non-system32 paths (e.g., antivirus, printer drivers, browser extensions). Build an allowlist of approved third-party DLL paths per environment. Alert on: unsigned + non-system path + high-privilege target process — this triple combination has very low FPR.

hypotheses.title: Impossible Travel — Same Account Authenticating from Geographically Distant IPs
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor is suspected of using stolen valid account credentials to authenticate from an IP geographically incompatible with the prior authentication event for the same account, indicating credential theft and abuse. Hunt for WinEvt 4624 (Type 3 or Type 10) logon events where the same user authenticates from two IPs whose geolocations represent travel time exceeding human possibility within the observed time window.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4624 — logon correlation
pivots.detail: EventID = 4624 AND LogonType IN (3, 10) — correlate TargetUserName across two events within a sliding 2-hour window where IpAddress field GeoIP lookup shows country/city change implying >1000 km travel. Alert when time delta between events < 60 minutes.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4625 — failed auths preceding success
pivots.detail: TargetUserName matches a prior 4625 (failure) from a foreign IP followed by 4624 (success) — password spray or brute-force pattern leading to successful compromise. Threshold: >=5 failures from same IP within 10 minutes, then success.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4648 — explicit credential use
pivots.detail: EventID = 4648 (logon with explicit credentials) where SubjectLogonId != TargetLogonId AND TargetServerName is a domain controller or file server — indicates pass-the-hash or RunAs-based lateral movement using valid account.

refs.label: CISA AA23-193A — Lazarus / valid accounts abuse
CISA AA24-038A — PRC actors valid accounts

hypotheses.fpr: VPN split tunneling, travel, and roaming workers legitimately produce geolocation shifts. Correlate against VPN/ZScaler authentication logs and HR travel data before escalating. Cloud identity providers (Okta, Entra ID) have built-in impossible-travel policies that should be the primary control; this hunt supplements on-prem AD.

hypotheses.title: Service Account Interactive Logon Outside Expected Baseline
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of using a compromised service account to perform interactive or network logons outside that account's normal usage pattern, leveraging the account's high privilege to move laterally or maintain persistence. Hunt for WinEvt 4624 events where the TargetUserName matches known service account naming conventions (svc*, *_svc, *service*) and LogonType is 2, 10, or 3 from an unexpected source workstation.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4624 — service account logon type
pivots.detail: EventID = 4624 AND LogonType IN (2, 10) AND TargetUserName MATCHES regex (svc.*|.*_svc|.*service.*|.*admin.*) AND WorkstationName NOT IN (known_jump_server_list) — interactive logon from a service account is almost always anomalous.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4672 — special privileges assigned
pivots.detail: EventID = 4672 (Special Privileges Assigned to New Logon) correlated to a service account logon in 4624 within the same LogonId. If PrivilegeList includes SeDebugPrivilege, SeTcbPrivilege, SeImpersonatePrivilege — escalate immediately.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4768 / 4769 — Kerberos for service accounts
pivots.detail: EventID = 4769 (Kerberos service ticket request) where AccountName matches svc* AND ClientAddress is a workstation not in the expected service account operational subnet. Kerberoasting leaves a trail here when SPN tickets are requested with RC4 (TicketEncryptionType = 0x17).

refs.label: CISA AA25-141A — Akira ransomware valid accounts

hypotheses.fpr: Some service accounts are legitimately used interactively by admins during maintenance windows. Baseline each svc account's historical LogonType distribution and source workstation list. Alert on deviations from the 90-day baseline. Patch-Tuesday maintenance windows are the most common FP source.

hypotheses.title: Default or Vendor Credential Use Against Network Services
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on a network is suspected of authenticating to network devices, cloud consoles, or internal services using default or factory-reset credentials that were never rotated, bypassing detection tuned for stolen enterprise credentials. Hunt for WinEvt 4624 or VPN/cloud authentication logs showing logon by accounts matching known default username patterns (admin, Administrator, guest, sa, root) from external or unexpected IP ranges.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4624 — default account names
pivots.detail: EventID = 4624 AND TargetUserName IN (Administrator, admin, Guest, DefaultAccount, WDAGUtilityAccount) AND LogonType = 3 AND IpAddress NOT IN (internal_CIDR_ranges) — external network logon with default account names.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4625 — failed default creds spray
pivots.detail: EventID = 4625 AND TargetUserName IN (admin, Administrator, sa, root, guest) AND IpAddress != local — repeated failures suggest credential stuffing. Threshold: >=10 failures in 5 minutes from same IP targeting default usernames.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4776 — NTLM with default accounts
pivots.detail: EventID = 4776 (NTLM credential validation) AND TargetUserName IN (Administrator, admin) AND Workstation shows external hostname or IP — NTLM authentication from outside the expected network boundary using default account.

refs.label: CISA AA24-038A — Volt Typhoon default creds

hypotheses.fpr: Built-in Administrator accounts are sometimes used by imaging/MDM solutions (SCCM, Autopilot). Enumerate legitimate uses during onboarding. Built-in Guest and DefaultAccount should never authenticate in production — zero-FPR alert candidates. WDAGUtilityAccount is used by Windows Sandbox; exclude that service context.

hypotheses.title: RDP Logon from Unexpected External Source to Non-Jump Hosts
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor is suspected of using stolen credentials or RDP brute-force to establish a Remote Desktop session directly to internal workstations or non-DMZ servers, bypassing jump-server controls. Hunt for WinEvt 4624 LogonType 10 events on hosts that are not designated RDP jump servers, especially where the source IP is outside the expected management subnet or is an anonymization service exit node.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4624 — Type 10 RemoteInteractive
pivots.detail: EventID = 4624 AND LogonType = 10 AND TargetServerName NOT IN (jump_server_list) AND IpAddress NOT IN (management_CIDR) — direct RDP to workstation from unexpected source. Enrich IpAddress against threat intel for TOR/VPN/proxy ASN.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4778 / 4779 — session reconnect/disconnect
pivots.detail: EventID = 4778 (Session Reconnected) on a host not in jump server list, OR multiple 4779 (Session Disconnected) followed by 4778 in rapid succession — indicates adversary cycling through RDP sessions. ClientName field resolving to foreign or mismatched hostname is a strong indicator.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 3 — RDP network connection
pivots.detail: Image = mstsc.exe AND DestinationPort = 3389 AND DestinationIp NOT IN (authorized_rdp_targets) — outbound RDP from unexpected source workstation, often indicating lateral movement hop. Also alert on alternate RDP ports (3390, 3391, 13389) to detect port-change evasion.

refs.label: CISA AA25-141A — Akira RDP initial access

hypotheses.fpr: Help desk and IT teams legitimately use RDP for support. Control via: jump-server allowlist in detection logic, business-hours baseline, and approved source IP ranges. RDP from management subnets to any internal host during business hours is a frequent FP; tune to off-hours or non-management source IPs first.

hypotheses.title: RDP Tunnel via Ngrok or Reverse Proxy Tool
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on a compromised Windows host is suspected of tunneling RDP traffic over an encrypted reverse proxy (ngrok, frp, Cloudflare Tunnel) to expose the internal host to external RDP access without requiring inbound firewall rules. Hunt for process creation of known tunneling binaries or DNS/network connections to tunnel provider infrastructure alongside a subsequent RDP session.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — tunnel binary
pivots.detail: Image endswith (ngrok.exe OR frpc.exe OR cloudflared.exe OR bore.exe OR rathole.exe) OR CommandLine contains (ngrok tcp 3389 OR frpc -c OR tunnel --proto tcp) — tunneling binary execution preceding an RDP logon event.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 22 — DNS to tunnel providers
pivots.detail: QueryName endswith (ngrok.io OR ngrok-agent.com OR tunnel.cloudflare.com OR bore.pub OR serveo.net OR localhost.run) — DNS queries to known reverse-proxy tunnel providers from workstation or server.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4624 — RDP after tunnel established
pivots.detail: EventID = 4624 AND LogonType = 10 within 60 seconds of an ngrok/frp DNS query or process start from the same host. Source IpAddress will appear as 127.0.0.1 or localhost (loopback) when tunnel is active — this loopback RDP source is a high-fidelity indicator.

hypotheses.fpr: Ngrok and Cloudflare Tunnel have legitimate developer and DevOps use cases. Baseline authorized use in CI/CD pipelines. Alert on execution from user %APPDATA%, %TEMP%, or Downloads folder rather than Program Files — that context has near-zero legitimate justification. Coordinate with IT to maintain an authorized tunneling tool allowlist.

hypotheses.title: Office Document Spawning Shell Process (Malicious Macro)
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor is suspected of delivering a weaponized Office document with an embedded macro that spawns a shell interpreter or living-off-the-land binary to download and execute a second-stage payload. Hunt for WinEvt 4688 or Sysmon EID 1 events where a shell process (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, wscript.exe, mshta.exe) is spawned by an Office application parent (winword.exe, excel.exe, outlook.exe).

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — Office parent spawning shell
pivots.detail: ParentImage IN (WINWORD.EXE, EXCEL.EXE, POWERPNT.EXE, OUTLOOK.EXE, MSPUB.EXE) AND Image IN (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, wscript.exe, cscript.exe, mshta.exe, bitsadmin.exe, certutil.exe, regsvr32.exe, rundll32.exe)

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 3 — outbound connection from Office
pivots.detail: Image IN (WINWORD.EXE, EXCEL.EXE) AND Initiated = true AND DestinationPort IN (80, 443, 8080) AND DestinationIp NOT IN (microsoft_CDN_ranges, o365_IP_ranges) — direct outbound HTTP from Office to unknown external IP indicates template injection or direct download cradle.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4688 — scripting engine child
pivots.detail: ProcessName IN (wscript.exe, cscript.exe) AND ParentProcessName IN (WINWORD.EXE, EXCEL.EXE, OUTLOOK.EXE) — Windows Script Host launched by Office. CommandLine of child process should be decoded; look for DownloadFile, Shell, Run, WScript.Shell patterns.

refs.label: CISA AA23-075A — phishing with macro delivery

hypotheses.fpr: Some Office add-ins and DDE data-refresh operations legitimately spawn scripts; these are typically signed, occur at predictable scheduled times, and target known internal servers. Allowlist by: signed child binary + known destination + scheduled task context. Raw cmd/powershell spawned interactively from Office outside of macro-approved policy is near-zero FPR.

hypotheses.title: Protected View Bypass — Office Document Edited Immediately After Download
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor is suspected of crafting a phishing attachment designed to social-engineer the victim into disabling Office Protected View or enabling macros, after which the payload executes. Hunt for Sysmon EID 11 showing an Office file written to disk from a mail client or browser (indicating attachment save), followed within 120 seconds by Sysmon EID 1 showing the same file opened by an Office application and spawning a child process.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 11 — attachment landing
pivots.detail: TargetFilename endswith (.doc OR .docm OR .xls OR .xlsm OR .xlsb OR .ppt OR .pptm OR .docx OR .one OR .lnk OR .iso OR .img) AND Image IN (OUTLOOK.EXE, chrome.exe, msedge.exe, firefox.exe, teams.exe) — file written to %TEMP%\Outlook\* or Downloads\ by a mail/browser process.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — child spawn within 120s
pivots.detail: ParentImage IN (WINWORD.EXE, EXCEL.EXE, POWERPNT.EXE, ONENOTE.EXE) AND Image IN (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, wscript.exe, mshta.exe) AND UtcTime within 120 seconds of EID 11 TargetFilename matching same base filename — tight time correlation is the key signal.

pivots.label: Registry — Mark of the Web
pivots.detail: HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Office\<version>\<app>\Security registry keys showing EnabledMacros or VBAWarnings changed from 2/3 to 1 within the same user session — indicates the user clicked 'Enable Content' under social engineering. Sysmon EID 13 on those registry paths confirms the change.

hypotheses.fpr: Users who open trusted documents from internal SharePoint or OneDrive sync may trigger file-write + open sequences. Key differentiator is the parent process for file creation: internal sync clients (OneDrive.exe) vs external mail clients (OUTLOOK.EXE). Tune on image that wrote the file — alert only when Outlook, browser, or Teams is the writer.

hypotheses.title: ISO/LNK Smuggling Chain Bypassing MOTW
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor is suspected of delivering phishing attachments as ISO or ZIP containers holding a shortcut (LNK) or DLL, bypassing Mark of the Web inheritance so macros or execution policies do not block payload execution once the container is mounted. Hunt for Sysmon EID 1 events where the executing image path is within a mounted ISO volume (drive letter with no fixed-disk backing) or a recently extracted ZIP in Downloads, spawning a shell or LOLBin.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — execution from mounted ISO
pivots.detail: CurrentDirectory matches regex ([D-Z]:\\[^\\]+\\) AND ParentImage = explorer.exe AND Image IN (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, rundll32.exe, mshta.exe, regsvr32.exe, wscript.exe) — child spawned by Explorer from a removable/optical volume letter is a strong ISO-mount execution indicator.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — LNK spawning LOLBin
pivots.detail: ParentImage = explorer.exe AND ParentCommandLine contains .lnk AND Image IN (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, mshta.exe, wscript.exe, cscript.exe, regsvr32.exe) — shortcut file directly spawning a shell. LNK files in mounted ISOs or ZIPs lack MOTW zone identifier.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 11 — ISO/IMG mount artifact
pivots.detail: TargetFilename endswith (.iso OR .img OR .vhd OR .vhdx) written to Downloads\ or %TEMP% by OUTLOOK.EXE, chrome.exe, or msedge.exe AND within 60 seconds a new volume appears (correlate with WinEvt 6416 — new device/volume mount).

hypotheses.fpr: CD/DVD and USB media (legitimate ISOs for software installation) also trigger Explorer-spawned processes from removable volumes. Suppress known software installer hashes (Windows ISOs, Oracle, VMware). Alert on: unknown publisher + shell spawn + no matching software deployment record in SCCM/Intune.

hypotheses.title: WMI Lateral Movement via wmic.exe or Win32_Process Create
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on a Windows network is suspected of using WMI Win32_Process Create — via wmic.exe or a scripting interface — to execute commands on remote hosts without deploying PSExec or other explicit lateral movement tools, leveraging built-in Windows management infrastructure. Hunt for Sysmon EID 1 showing wmic.exe with /node: or process call create arguments, and for WinEvt 4688 showing WMI-spawned processes (parent = WmiPrvSE.exe) on target hosts.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — wmic with /node
pivots.detail: Image endswith wmic.exe AND CommandLine contains (/node: OR /node:"*") AND CommandLine contains (process OR create OR call) — remote WMI command invocation. Further narrow: CommandLine contains (cmd, powershell, rundll32, regsvr32, certutil) as the spawned process.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — WmiPrvSE parent on target
pivots.detail: ParentImage = WmiPrvSE.exe AND Image IN (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, cscript.exe, rundll32.exe, mshta.exe) — WMI provider host spawning a shell is the target-side indicator of remote WMI execution. This is the highest-fidelity WMI lateral movement signal.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4688 — WmiPrvSE child
pivots.detail: EventID = 4688 AND CreatorProcessName endswith WmiPrvSE.exe AND NewProcessName IN (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, net.exe, whoami.exe, ipconfig.exe) — process creation audit log equivalent of the Sysmon EID 1 pivot above. Requires command-line auditing enabled via auditpol.

refs.label: CISA AA24-038A — Volt Typhoon WMI abuse

hypotheses.fpr: System Center Configuration Manager (SCCM) and other management platforms use WMI extensively. WmiPrvSE.exe spawning msiexec.exe or cscript.exe from C:\Windows\System32 for known deployment tasks is a common FP. Suppress by: parent-child pair + known deployment hash or signed binary path. Alert primarily on: WmiPrvSE spawning cmd/powershell with interactive-looking command lines.

hypotheses.title: WMI Persistence via __EventFilter and ActiveScriptEventConsumer
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on a Windows host is suspected of establishing WMI-based persistence using __EventFilter, __EventConsumer, and __FilterToConsumerBinding objects to execute a payload automatically on system events (e.g., logon, interval, process start) without a scheduled task or registry run key. Hunt for Sysmon EID 19, 20, and 21 showing creation or modification of WMI subscriptions, especially ActiveScript or CommandLine consumer types executing from unusual paths.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 19 — WMI EventFilter
pivots.detail: EventType = WmiEventFilter AND Query contains (SELECT * FROM __InstanceCreationEvent OR SELECT * FROM Win32_LogonSession OR SELECT * FROM __TimerEvent) AND Name NOT IN (known_management_tool_filter_names)

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 20 — WMI Consumer
pivots.detail: EventType = WmiEventConsumer AND ConsumerType IN (ActiveScriptEventConsumer, CommandLineEventConsumer) AND Destination contains (powershell OR cmd OR wscript OR cscript OR mshta OR rundll32 OR %TEMP% OR %APPDATA%)

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 21 — Binding created
pivots.detail: EventType = WmiEventConsumerToFilter — any new FilterToConsumerBinding where the Consumer references an ActiveScript or CommandLine consumer not in the approved baseline should be investigated. Correlate EID 21 with preceding EID 19 and 20 within the same session.

hypotheses.fpr: SCCM, Symantec Endpoint, and some Microsoft monitoring agents create legitimate WMI subscriptions. Run a baseline of all EventFilter/EventConsumer objects in the environment before deploying detection. Any new subscription not matching the baseline is suspicious — FPR is very low in well-managed environments with a subscription inventory.

hypotheses.title: WMI Used for Defense Evasion — Executing Payload via Scripting Consumer
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on a Windows system is suspected of using the WMI ActiveScriptEventConsumer to execute a VBScript or JScript payload triggered by a system event, bypassing application whitelisting controls that do not monitor WMI-initiated script execution. Hunt for WinEvt 4104 (ScriptBlock) or process creation logs showing wscript.exe or cscript.exe spawned by WmiPrvSE.exe with a script path in a temp or user-writable directory.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — wscript/cscript via WmiPrvSE
pivots.detail: ParentImage = WmiPrvSE.exe AND Image IN (wscript.exe, cscript.exe, powershell.exe) AND CommandLine contains (%TEMP%\ OR %APPDATA%\ OR C:\ProgramData\ OR C:\Users\Public\)

pivots.label: WinEvt 4104 — script content inspection
pivots.detail: EventID = 4104 AND ScriptBlockText contains (WScript.Shell OR CreateObject OR Shell.Run OR Net.WebClient OR DownloadFile) — script blocks triggered by WMI consumers often contain dropper or downloader logic.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 7 — DLL loaded by WmiPrvSE
pivots.detail: Image = WmiPrvSE.exe AND ImageLoaded NOT startswith C:\Windows\System32 AND Signed = false — unsigned or side-loaded DLL loaded into the WMI provider host indicates a more advanced WMI abuse variant (e.g., MOF file compiled DLL consumer).

hypotheses.fpr: WMI-initiated scripts from C:\Windows\System32 or signed application paths are usually legitimate (antivirus, SCCM). Alert specifically on script paths in user-writable locations. WMI spawning wscript.exe from %TEMP% has near-zero legitimate justification in production environments.

hypotheses.title: Scheduled Task Created to Execute from Staging Path
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on a Windows host is suspected of creating a scheduled task via schtasks.exe or the Task Scheduler COM API to persist a payload located in a user-writable or temp directory, ensuring execution on a recurring basis or at logon. Hunt for WinEvt 4698 (task created) and Sysmon EID 1 (schtasks.exe /create) events where the task action command resolves to a path in %TEMP%, %APPDATA%, C:\ProgramData, or C:\Users\Public.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4698 — task created
pivots.detail: EventID = 4698 AND TaskContent contains (cmd.exe OR powershell.exe OR wscript.exe OR mshta.exe OR rundll32.exe OR regsvr32.exe) AND TaskContent contains (%TEMP% OR %APPDATA% OR C:\ProgramData OR C:\Users\Public OR C:\Windows\Temp)

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — schtasks /create CLI
pivots.detail: Image endswith schtasks.exe AND CommandLine contains /create AND CommandLine contains (/tr OR /xml) AND CommandLine contains (%TEMP% OR AppData OR ProgramData OR Public) — command-line scheduled task creation targeting a staging path.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4698 + 4702 — task modified within 60s
pivots.detail: EID 4698 (created) followed by EID 4702 (updated) within 60 seconds for the same task name — adversary creating then immediately modifying a task is a common pattern from automated post-exploitation scripts (Cobalt Strike, Metasploit) that create then adjust task parameters.

hypotheses.fpr: IT automation, patch management (WSUS, SCCM), AV products, and backup agents all create scheduled tasks. Maintain an approved task inventory. Alert specifically on: task action path in user-writable directory + created by a non-SYSTEM, non-service account interactively. Tasks created by cmd.exe or powershell.exe as the creating process are higher fidelity than those created by system services.

hypotheses.title: Scheduled Task Executing Encoded or Downloaded Command
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on a Windows system is suspected of creating a scheduled task whose action includes an encoded PowerShell command or a download-then-execute one-liner, enabling fileless or staged payload delivery at scheduled intervals. Hunt for WinEvt 4698 where the TaskContent XML action element contains Base64-encoded strings, download cradle keywords, or obfuscated command flags.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4698 — encoded or cradle in task XML
pivots.detail: EventID = 4698 AND TaskContent contains (-enc OR -EncodedCommand OR DownloadString OR DownloadFile OR IEX OR Invoke-Expression OR FromBase64String OR bitsadmin OR certutil.*decode) — scheduled task action containing download or decode logic.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — task execution at trigger
pivots.detail: ParentImage = taskeng.exe OR ParentImage = svchost.exe AND ParentCommandLine contains Schedule AND Image = powershell.exe AND CommandLine contains (-enc OR -nop OR bypass OR IEX) — task-triggered PowerShell with evasion flags.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4700 / 4701 — task enabled/disabled cycling
pivots.detail: EID 4700 (task enabled) followed by EID 4701 (task disabled) in rapid cycles — an adversary testing or cycling a scheduled task to check execution. Also alert on EID 4700 for a task not in the approved baseline being enabled by a non-privileged account.

hypotheses.fpr: Legitimate admin tasks may use PowerShell but rarely require encoding. SCCM deployment scripts running via scheduled tasks sometimes embed encoded PS; these are typically created by the SYSTEM account from a known SCCM server. Filter by: task created by SYSTEM + TaskContent shows known SCCM/Intune publishing source. Encoded commands in tasks created by user accounts are near-zero FPR.

hypotheses.title: Registry Run Key Modification for Persistence
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on a Windows host is suspected of adding or modifying registry Run or RunOnce keys to execute a payload at user logon or system startup, establishing persistence without creating a scheduled task or service. Hunt for Sysmon EID 13 events modifying HKCU or HKLM Run keys where the target value data points to a binary in a user-writable or staging path.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 13 — Run key set
pivots.detail: EventType = SetValue AND TargetObject contains (\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run OR \SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce OR \SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run) AND Details contains (%TEMP% OR %APPDATA% OR C:\Users\Public OR C:\ProgramData OR \AppData\Roaming OR \AppData\Local)

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 13 — Run key unusual binary
pivots.detail: Same TargetObject as above AND Details endswith (.exe OR .dll OR .vbs OR .js OR .bat OR .ps1 OR .lnk) AND Image NOT IN (msiexec.exe, setup.exe, installer binaries signed by known vendors) — run key value set by a non-installer process is high confidence.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4657 — registry value modification
pivots.detail: EventID = 4657 (Registry value modified) AND ObjectName contains CurrentVersion\Run AND NewValue NOT IN (approved_persistence_baseline) — requires Object Access Auditing on registry keys. Provides actor AccountName and ProcessName for attribution.

hypotheses.fpr: Software installers routinely write Run keys — these are signed, installed from Program Files, and occur during known installation windows. Allowlist by: signed binary at C:\Program Files\ or C:\Windows\. The highest FPR source is legitimate apps (Spotify, Teams, OneDrive) adding update helpers to Run. Maintain a baseline of approved Run key values and alert on any deviation pointing to user-writable paths.

hypotheses.title: Security Provider or Debugger Registry Keys Tampered for Persistence or Credential Access
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on a Windows system is suspected of modifying HKLM Security Packages, Authentication Packages, or Image File Execution Options (IFEO) registry keys to load a malicious DLL through the SSP/AP interface or to hijack a target binary via the Debugger subkey. Hunt for Sysmon EID 13 on HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa and HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options where the value is changed to include an unusual module or path.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 13 — LSA Security Packages
pivots.detail: EventType = SetValue AND TargetObject contains (\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\Security Packages OR \SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\Authentication Packages OR \SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\OSConfig\Security Packages) AND Details NOT IN (known_approved_SSP_list) — adversary-added SSP/AP DLL persists across reboots and loads into lsass.exe.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 13 — IFEO Debugger subkey
pivots.detail: EventType = SetValue AND TargetObject contains \SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options AND TargetObject endswith \Debugger AND Details NOT IN (ntsd.exe, windbg.exe, cdb.exe at known debugger paths) — IFEO Debugger set to an attacker binary causes it to launch instead of the target application (Sticky Keys hijack, etc.).

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 7 — unexpected DLL loaded into lsass
pivots.detail: Image = lsass.exe AND ImageLoaded NOT IN (known_lsass_dll_baseline) AND Signed = false OR SignatureStatus != Valid — newly loaded unsigned DLL into lsass after a reboot following LSA package registry modification confirms SSP/AP injection.

hypotheses.fpr: Third-party MFA solutions and smart card middleware legitimately register Authentication Packages. Baseline all LSA Security Package entries and treat any new value not matching approved packages as critical. IFEO Debugger keys set by Visual Studio for managed debugging are common in dev environments — exclude VS install paths. In production, both are near-zero FPR.

hypotheses.title: DisableAntiSpyware or DisableRealtimeMonitoring Registry Keys Modified
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on a Windows host is suspected of setting Windows Defender registry keys to disable real-time protection or reporting, disabling a primary defense layer before deploying ransomware or a persistent implant. Hunt for Sysmon EID 13 events where HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender or HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows Defender keys are modified to set Disable* values to 1.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 13 — Defender policy keys
pivots.detail: EventType = SetValue AND TargetObject contains (\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender OR \SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Real-Time Protection) AND TargetObject endswith (DisableAntiSpyware OR DisableRealtimeMonitoring OR DisableBehaviorMonitoring OR DisableOnAccessProtection OR DisableScanOnRealtimeEnable) AND Details = DWORD (0x00000001)

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — reg.exe or PowerShell setting the key
pivots.detail: Image IN (reg.exe, powershell.exe) AND CommandLine contains (DisableRealtimeMonitoring OR DisableAntiSpyware OR Set-MpPreference.*-Disable OR Add-MpPreference) AND CommandLine contains (1 OR $true OR Disable) — command line that modifies Defender policy.

pivots.label: WinEvt 5001 / 5004 / 5007 — Defender config changes
pivots.detail: EventID = 5007 in the Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational log: 'Changed configuration' — logs the old and new value for Defender configuration changes. Parse OldValue vs NewValue to confirm a disable action. EID 5001 = Defender real-time protection disabled.

refs.label: CISA AA25-141A — Akira AV disable via registry

hypotheses.fpr: Intune/SCCM-managed Defender policies deliver changes via HKLM\Policies path, but changes are applied by trusted system processes (MsMpEng.exe, CSE DLL) not by cmd.exe or powershell.exe directly. Alert when Image = cmd.exe, powershell.exe, or reg.exe makes the change — that context is near-zero FPR in production. MDM policy changes from SYSTEM context are typically safe to suppress.

hypotheses.title: Windows Defender Disabled via PowerShell Set-MpPreference
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on a Windows host is suspected of using PowerShell's Set-MpPreference or Add-MpPreference cmdlets to disable Windows Defender real-time monitoring, IOAV protection, or script scanning prior to deploying ransomware or a persistent implant. Hunt for Sysmon EID 1 and EID 4104 events showing Set-MpPreference with disabling parameters executed by non-SYSTEM accounts or from unexpected parent processes.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — Set-MpPreference command line
pivots.detail: Image endswith powershell.exe AND CommandLine contains Set-MpPreference AND CommandLine contains (-DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true OR -DisableBehaviorMonitoring $true OR -DisableIOAVProtection $true OR -DisableScriptScanning $true OR -DisableAntiSpyware $true OR -MAPSReporting 0)

pivots.label: PS EID 4104 — script block inspection
pivots.detail: EventID = 4104 AND ScriptBlockText contains (Set-MpPreference OR Add-MpPreference) AND ScriptBlockText contains (Disable OR $true OR -ExclusionPath OR -ExclusionProcess) — catches encoded or multi-stage scripts that invoke the cmdlet indirectly.

pivots.label: WinEvt 5007 — Defender operational log
pivots.detail: Provider = Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender AND EventID = 5007 AND Message contains 'MALWAREPROTECTION_CONFIG_CHANGED' AND NewValue contains (DisableRealtimeMonitoring = 0x1 OR DisableAntiSpyware = 0x1) — Defender's own log confirming the disable action, independent of process audit.

hypotheses.fpr: Legitimate IT admin scripts during maintenance may temporarily disable Defender components; these should be gated by a change management record and run from an approved admin workstation under a service account. In environments with third-party AV, Defender is sometimes policy-disabled — suppress when disabled by MsMpEng.exe or SYSTEM from a known MDM process tree. User or attacker context executing these cmdlets has near-zero FPR.

hypotheses.title: EDR/AV Driver or Service Stopped via sc.exe or WDAC Bypass
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on a Windows host with elevated privileges is suspected of terminating or unloading an EDR or AV product's kernel driver or service using sc.exe, net stop, or a vulnerable driver exploit (BYOVD) to blind defensive tooling prior to ransomware deployment. Hunt for Sysmon EID 1 showing sc.exe stop/delete targeting known security product service names, and for WinEvt 7036 (service state change) affecting security services.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — sc.exe stop/delete security service
pivots.detail: Image endswith sc.exe AND CommandLine contains (stop OR delete OR disable OR config.*start=disabled) AND CommandLine contains known_security_service_names — e.g., MsMpSvc, WinDefend, SentinelAgent, CylanceSvc, CbDefense, CSFalconService, McShield, ekrn, avp.

pivots.label: WinEvt 7036 — service state change
pivots.detail: EventID = 7036 (Service Control Manager) AND Message contains (WinDefend OR SentinelAgent OR CSFalconService OR CylanceSvc OR MsMpEng OR bdagent) AND Message contains stopped — security service stopped. Cross-correlate with the process that issued the stop command via EventID 7040 or Sysmon EID 1 timeline.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — BYOVD vulnerable driver load
pivots.detail: Image IN (fltMC.exe, sc.exe) AND CommandLine contains (load OR start) AND CommandLine contains driver name of known BYOVD drivers (mhyprot2.sys, gdrv.sys, DBUtil_2_3.sys, zamguard64.sys, procexp152.sys) — loading a vulnerable third-party driver to kill EDR via kernel-level call.

hypotheses.fpr: Legitimate EDR upgrades or OS reinstallation tasks may stop and restart security services; these are gated by change management and run from SYSTEM or a designated service account. Alert when the stopping process parent is cmd.exe, powershell.exe, or a C2 implant process rather than a signed services orchestrator. Correlate with the change management calendar for near-zero FPR in production.

hypotheses.title: Security Tool Exclusion Added to Defender or Third-Party AV
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on a Windows host is suspected of adding file path, process, or extension exclusions to Windows Defender or a third-party AV configuration, allowing malicious payloads to execute in an excluded directory without triggering signature or behavioral detection. Hunt for Sysmon EID 1 showing Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath or registry writes to Defender Exclusion keys, particularly when the excluded path matches a known staging location.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — Add-MpPreference exclusion
pivots.detail: Image endswith powershell.exe AND CommandLine contains Add-MpPreference AND CommandLine contains (-ExclusionPath OR -ExclusionProcess OR -ExclusionExtension) AND CommandLine contains (%TEMP% OR %APPDATA% OR C:\ProgramData OR C:\Users\Public OR C:\Windows\Temp)

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 13 — Defender exclusion registry key
pivots.detail: EventType = SetValue AND TargetObject contains \SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Exclusions\Paths AND Details contains (%TEMP% OR C:\ProgramData OR C:\Users\Public OR user-controlled path) — registry write adding an exclusion. Requires Sysmon monitoring registry value set events.

pivots.label: WinEvt 5007 — Defender config: ExclusionPath added
pivots.detail: EventID = 5007 AND Message contains ExclusionPath AND NewValue contains a path not in the approved exclusion baseline — Defender operational log records all configuration changes including exclusion additions. Compare NewValue against an approved exclusion allowlist.

hypotheses.fpr: Enterprise software deployments (SQL Server, Oracle, backup agents) legitimately add Defender exclusions during installation, typically via SYSTEM-context installers from C:\Program Files. Alert when: exclusion path is in a user-writable directory + added by a user-context process (not SYSTEM or a signed installer). Adding exclusions for paths already containing a newly dropped executable is a near-certain indicator — correlate file creation events.
